passages.t: A great catch, and ‘Go away from me’
passages.happening:
Jesus is standing by the lake, and the crowd is pressing in to hear the word of God. He sees two boats on the shore. The fishermen are washing their nets. He gets into Simon's boat, asks him to push out a little, and sits down to teach the people from the water.

When he finishes, he tells Simon, “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch” (verse 4). “Master,” Simon replies, “we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets” (verse 5).

They catch so many fish that the nets begin to tear. They wave to their partners in the other boat, and both boats are filled until they begin to sink.

Simon falls at Jesus' knees. “Go away from me, Lord,” he says, “for I am a sinful man” (verse 8). He and all with him are astonished, and so are his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus says to Simon. “From now on you will catch men” (verse 10). They bring the boats to shore, leave everything, and follow him.
passages.hearers:
Luke calls the Sea of Galilee ‘the Lake of Gennesaret’. Gennesaret was a fertile plain on its north-west shore. Matthew, Mark and John call it a ‘sea’; only Luke calls it a lake. It is a freshwater lake, and fishing was its trade. A fishing boat from about the time of Jesus was found in its mud in 1986, during a drought. It is about eight metres long, big enough for a crew and a heavy catch.

Fishermen on the lake often worked through the night. Many think this was because fish could see the nets in daylight. So Simon's reply makes sense. These are experts. They have worked all night, the best time, and caught nothing. Now a teacher from a hill village tells them to try again, in daylight, in deep water. Simon's ‘But because You say so’ is real trust.

Mark and Matthew tell the call of these fishermen more briefly, by the shore (Mark 1:16-20; Matthew 4:18-22), and their notes explain it. Luke tells it differently. In Luke, Simon has already heard Jesus teach and seen his mother-in-law healed (4:38-39). Then comes the catch, and only then the call. Luke shows why these men were ready to leave everything.

Notice how Simon speaks. First he says ‘Master’, a word for a man in charge. After the catch he says ‘Lord’. Luke also calls him ‘Simon Peter’ here for the first time, at the moment he falls down.

The word Jesus uses for ‘catch’ is unusual. It means to catch alive. It was used of taking prisoners alive in war rather than killing them. Fish are caught to die. People are caught for life.
passages.ot:
Peter's cry recalls Isaiah's. When Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple, he said, “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). Then God cleansed him and sent him. Peter sees God's power at work in Jesus and feels his own sin. Then Jesus says ‘Do not be afraid’ and gives him work. It is the pattern of a prophet's call.

Jeremiah spoke of God sending “for many fishermen” (Jeremiah 16:16), but there they catch people for judgment. Jesus turns the picture around.

‘Do not be afraid’ is what God and his angels say again and again in Scripture when people meet him: to Abraham (Genesis 15:1), to Mary (Luke 1:30), to the shepherds (Luke 2:10).
passages.hard:
John's Gospel tells of another huge catch, after the resurrection, when Peter has denied Jesus (John 21:1-14). Some scholars think Luke and John tell one event, placed at different times. Others think they are two catches, and that the second one, by the risen Jesus, deliberately recalls the first. In Luke the nets begin to tear and Peter asks Jesus to leave. In John the net holds and Peter jumps into the water to reach him. Nothing in the faith depends on settling which view is right.

Some have read this story as a promise of business success to those who obey Jesus. The story points the other way. The fishermen pull in the best catch of their lives, and then leave it on the beach.
passages.asks: Peter felt his sin most when Jesus was being most generous. Jesus did not go away. He said ‘Do not be afraid’ and gave him a job. If you feel too sinful to come near God, you are in good company. What would it mean to hear ‘Do not be afraid’ said to you, and to take the next step anyway?

passages.happening:
In one of the towns, a man “covered with leprosy” (verse 12) sees Jesus, falls on his face, and begs him, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean” (verse 12).

Jesus reaches out his hand and touches him. “I am willing,” he says. “Be clean!” (verse 13). At once the leprosy leaves him.

Jesus tells him not to tell anyone, but to show himself to the priest and make the offering Moses commanded for cleansing, “as a testimony to them” (verse 14). Even so, the news about Jesus spreads further, and great crowds come to hear him and be healed. “Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 1:40-45; Matthew 8:1-4), and their notes explain what ‘leprosy’ meant in the Bible: not only the disease we call leprosy today, but many skin conditions. The law made such a person unclean. He had to live apart, wear torn clothes, and call out ‘Unclean’ so that others would keep away. Anyone who touched him became unclean too.

Luke says the man was ‘covered with’ leprosy. This was no small patch. He was as sick, and as shut out, as a man could be.

Jesus touched him before he spoke. He could have healed him with a word. For a man no one had touched in a long time, the touch came first.

Sending him to the priest was not a formality. Only a priest could declare him clean. That declaration let him go home, go back to worship, and live among people again.

Luke adds one more line: Jesus often went off alone to pray. The more the crowds grew, the more he withdrew. Luke shows Jesus praying again and again.
passages.ot:
The law of the outcast is in Leviticus: “He must live alone in a place outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). The offering for cleansing is in Leviticus 14. Jesus does not break the law here. He sends the man to keep it.

In the Old Testament, healing leprosy was something only God could do. When Naaman came, the king of Israel cried, “Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?” (2 Kings 5:7). Luke has just mentioned Naaman (4:27).
passages.hard:
The leper was sure Jesus could heal him. He was not sure Jesus would. Many sick people today ask the same question, and some have prayed for healing that did not come.

It needs to be said plainly, here at the start of these healing stories, and it holds for every one of them. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul begged the Lord three times to take away his ‘thorn in the flesh’ and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). He left his friend Trophimus “sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20). He told Timothy to take a little wine for his “frequent ailments” (1 Timothy 5:23). None of these men are blamed. Faith is trust in a person, not a payment that buys a cure. Seeking a doctor is not a failure of faith either; Paul called his friend Luke “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14).
passages.asks: The man asked, ‘Are you willing?’ Jesus answered with a touch. Do you believe God is able but doubt that he wants to help you? Bring the question to him as the man did. And notice that Jesus, with crowds waiting, kept slipping away to pray.

passages.happening:
One day Jesus is teaching. Pharisees and teachers of the law are sitting there. People have come from every village of Galilee and Judea, and from Jerusalem. “And the power of the Lord was present for Him to heal the sick” (verse 17).

Some men bring a paralysed man on a mat. They cannot get through the crowd, so they go up on the roof and lower him “through the tiles” (verse 19), right in front of Jesus.

Seeing their faith, Jesus says, “Friend, your sins are forgiven” (verse 20). The scribes and Pharisees think, ‘Who is this man who speaks blasphemy? Who can forgive sins but God alone?’

Jesus knows their thoughts. He asks which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven’ or ‘Get up and walk’. Then, “so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on the earth to forgive sins” (verse 24), he tells the man to get up, take his mat, and go home. The man stands up at once and goes home praising God. Everyone is amazed: “We have seen remarkable things today” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 2:1-12; Matthew 9:1-8), and their notes tell about the houses and the roof. Mark says the friends dug through the roof. Luke speaks of tiles, the kind of roof his readers elsewhere in the Roman world would picture.

This is the first time the Pharisees appear in Luke. They were a group devoted to keeping God's law carefully in daily life, and they were respected by ordinary people. Teachers of the law, or scribes, were experts in the law. Luke says people had come from far away, even from Jerusalem. News of Jesus had reached the capital.

Mark has Jesus call the man ‘Son’. Luke has ‘Friend’. In Luke's Greek the word is simply ‘Man’, a plain way of speaking to someone.

The scribes are not being petty. They are right that only God can forgive sins against God. That is what makes Jesus' words so startling.

‘Son of Man’ is the name Jesus uses for himself most often. In everyday Aramaic it could simply mean ‘a man’. But it also recalls a figure in the book of Daniel. Here Jesus claims that this Son of Man has authority ‘on the earth’ to do what only God does.

Luke's word ‘today’ comes back in verse 26. It is one of his favourite words for the moment God's promise arrives.
passages.ot:
Daniel saw in a vision “One like the Son of Man” who came with the clouds of heaven and “was given dominion” (Daniel 7:13-14). That is the background of Jesus' title.

The psalm puts forgiving and healing side by side: the LORD “forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases” (Psalm 103:3). Isaiah promised a day when “the lame will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6). The scribes knew that only God forgives. The prophets said God would one day come to heal his people.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus claim to be God here, or does he only announce God's forgiveness, as a prophet might? Luke lets the scribes say the question out loud: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (verse 21). Jesus does not correct them. Instead he heals the man as proof that his word has weight. Luke wants the reader to feel the force of the question and to follow it to its end.

Was the man paralysed because of his sins? The passage does not say so. Many people then assumed that sickness came from sin, but Jesus warned against that idea (John 9:2-3). He forgave the man first because forgiveness was the deeper need, not because his sin had caused his illness. No one should be told that their illness or disability is a punishment.
passages.asks: The man could not come to Jesus by himself. His friends carried him, and they would not let a crowd stop them. Jesus saw ‘their faith’. Who has carried you? And who could you carry to Jesus, by prayer or by help, when they cannot come alone?

passages.t: Levi, and a banquet with sinners
passages.happening:
Jesus goes out and sees a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” he says (verse 27). Levi gets up, leaves everything, and follows him.

Then Levi holds a great banquet for Jesus at his house. A large crowd of tax collectors and others are eating with them. The Pharisees and their scribes complain to Jesus' disciples: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” (verse 30).

Jesus answers, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance” (verses 31-32).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 2:13-17; Matthew 9:9-13), and their notes explain tax collectors. Capernaum sat near a border, on a road used by traders. Levi was most likely a toll collector, taking customs on goods for Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee. Tax collectors had a name for taking more than was owed, and many Jews saw them as traitors who grew rich off their neighbours.

Matthew's Gospel calls this tax collector Matthew (Matthew 9:9). Most think Levi and Matthew are two names for one man, but Luke does not say so.

Luke adds two things. Levi ‘left everything’, the same words used of the fishermen in verse 11. And he threw a ‘great banquet’. A man who had made his money at others' cost now spends it to bring his friends to Jesus.

In that world, sharing a meal meant acceptance. The Pharisees kept careful rules about food and purity. To them, eating with such people seemed to approve of how they lived.

Only Luke has the last two words, ‘to repentance’. Jesus does welcome sinners. He also calls them to turn around. Levi's banquet is the joy of a man who has already done so.
passages.ot:
‘Complained’ is a grumbling word. It recalls Israel in the desert, when Moses told the people that the LORD “has heard your grumbling against Him” (Exodus 16:7). The same complaint comes back later in Luke, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (15:2).

God asks through Ezekiel, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” And he answers his own question: “Wouldn't I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). Jesus the doctor came for exactly that.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus mean that some people are righteous and do not need him? No. His words have a sharp edge. Those who think they are healthy will not call a doctor. The Pharisees' problem is not that they are too good, but that they do not see their own need.

It is easy to make the Pharisees cartoon villains. They cared about holiness, and many good people share their worry about keeping company with the compromised. Jesus' answer is not that holiness does not matter. It is that holiness, in him, goes out to heal the sick instead of keeping away from them.
passages.asks: The first great feast Luke tells of in Jesus' work is at a tax collector's house. If you feel unwelcome in church because of your past or your job, notice where Jesus chose to eat. And if you are the one who keeps your distance from ‘that kind of person’, ask what kind of doctor stays away from the sick.

passages.happening:
They say to Jesus, “John's disciples and those of the Pharisees frequently fast and pray, but Yours keep on eating and drinking” (verse 33).

Jesus answers, “Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast” (verses 34-35).

He tells them a parable. No one tears a piece from a new garment to patch an old one; that ruins the new and does not match the old. No one pours new wine into old wineskins; the skins burst and the wine is lost. New wine goes into new skins. “And no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is better’” (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this too (Mark 2:18-22; Matthew 9:14-17), and their notes explain the fasting, the wedding and the wineskins. The law commanded only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement. Many devout people fasted more often. A wedding was a feast that could last for days, and fasting at one would be rude.

Wine was kept in leather skins. New wine was still fermenting and stretched its container. An old skin was dry and stiff, and it burst.

Luke tells the patch picture his own way. In Mark, a new patch tears an old coat. In Luke, someone cuts up a new coat to patch an old one, and ruins both. You cannot add Jesus to an old pattern as a small repair.

Only Luke has verse 39. It is a dry, wry comment. People who like the old wine do not want to try the new. Jesus knows that many will refuse what he brings simply because they are used to the old. The oldest copies say ‘The old is good’; later copies say ‘better’. A few old copies leave the verse out.
passages.ot: In the Old Testament, God speaks of himself as the husband of his people. Isaiah says the LORD is Israel's husband and Maker (Isaiah 54:5). In Hosea God says, “I will betroth you to Me forever” (Hosea 2:19). Jesus calls himself the bridegroom. The prophets also pictured the age to come as a time when “the mountains will drip with sweet wine” (Amos 9:13; Joel 3:18).
passages.hard:
‘The bridegroom will be taken from them’ is an early hint that Jesus will die. The joy of the wedding already has a shadow over it.

Does Jesus forbid fasting? No. He says his followers will fast when he is taken away. Christians have fasted ever since, in many ways. Nor is this saying a rule about worship styles or church methods, as it is sometimes used. Its subject is the newness of God's kingdom arriving in Jesus.
passages.asks: ‘The old is good enough’ is a comfortable thing to say. What in your faith have you grown so used to that you would rather not taste anything new from God? And is your faith more like a wedding or a funeral?
